cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell: Non-cohort qualitative case study design; participant refusal rates or any drop-off across the two fieldwork phases (2015-2016 and 2016-2018) are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable (qualitative design): The study does not estimate quantitative causal effects, though it qualitatively contextualizes structural differences in class, topography, developer governance, and patronage networks between Izbet ElHaggana and New Cairo.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate (qualitative institutional description): Legal and administrative arrangements—including the 2004 and 2006 presidential decrees corporatizing provincial utilities and tariff regulation, the 2008 governorate policy and 2013 Greater Cairo Water Company installation of legal metered pipes in Izbet ElHaggana, and New Urban Communities Authority / private developer governance in New Cairo—are traced via secondary literature, policy reports, and interviews rather than primary statutory or doctrinal coding.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern (Can't tell on data collection/analysis rigor): Data collection was asymmetric across sites (in-person visits and narrative walks in Izbet ElHaggana in 2015-2016 versus virtual/abroad interviews and the author's own lived experience for New Cairo in 2016-2018), and interview guides, recording/transcription, translation from Arabic, and qualitative coding procedures are unreported.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Qualitative experiential measurement: Water service outcomes (supply cutoffs, duration of shortages, yellowed water quality, storage/bribery expenses, and gehood zateya repair practices) rely on resident accounts, field photographs/observations, and local media reports rather than standardized hydraulic or water-quality measurements.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern (Can't tell): No interview protocol or systematic coding framework is reported to assess selective quotation across the 72 interviews, although the narrative candidly reports disconfirming nuances such as intra-community free-riding/conflict over informal pipe funds and developer-utility blame-shifting.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (Can't tell on recruitment): While purposive selection of two contrasting Cairo settlements (informal Izbet ElHaggana vs. elite ElTagammo' ElKhames) fits the comparative theoretical aims, the paper provides no information on how the 72 interviewees were identified or recruited, site-specific sample counts, or how reliance on virtual interviews and personal familiarity in New Cairo shaped participant selection.

domain_ratings.justification: The author explicitly formulates two core research aims: interrogating how water infrastructure repair operates within hybrid configurations under formalization and privatization, and examining how informal everyday politics (gehood zateya) shape state-society relations across marginalized and elite areas of Cairo.

A qualitative methodology combining interviews, narrative walks, field observations, and archival research is well suited to investigating everyday socio-technical repair practices, informal patronage networks, and discursive narratives of infrastructural decay.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Research design appropriate to address aims
domain_ratings.justification: The comparative two-case study design contrasting an unplanned low-income settlement (Izbet ElHaggana) with an elite/middle-class suburban district (ElTagammo' ElKhames in New Cairo) directly addresses the objective of analyzing hybrid repair across class, legal status, and urban space, though the reason for shifting from Cairo fieldwork (Phase 1) to UK-based/virtual research (Phase 2) is left implicit.
domain_ratings.where_found: Research methods and context & Research sites (PDF Pages 8-10)

domain_ratings.justification: Although 72 interviews were conducted with residents, water-sector businessmen, civil society actors, urban activists, and government employees, the paper gives no account of how participants were sampled or approached, how interviews were distributed across the two sites and stakeholder groups, or whether prospective participants declined.
domain_ratings.where_found: Research methods and context (PDF Page 8); Notes 2-27 (PDF Pages 19-20)

domain_ratings.justification: Data collection modes (2015-2016 Cairo site visits, interviews, and narrative walks; 2016-2018 US/UK archival research and virtual/London interviews; 72 interviews total) and limitations of virtual interviewing are briefly stated, but there is no description of interview guides, audio recording or note-taking, Arabic-to-English translation, data saturation, or how methodological asymmetry between in-person ElHaggana fieldwork and remote New Cairo interviews affected comparability.
domain_ratings.where_found: Research methods and context (PDF Page 8); Results (PDF Pages 10-16)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered (reflexivity)
domain_ratings.justification: The author briefly notes having prior experiential knowledge and personal experiences in gated and non-gated communities in New Cairo (PDF Page 8) and prior research in ElHaggana (PDF Page 10), but does not critically examine her own class/insider-outsider positionality, power relations with marginalized versus elite informants, or potential bias from drawing on personal residential experience as evidence.
domain_ratings.where_found: Research methods and context (PDF Page 8); Results (PDF Page 10)

domain_ratings.justification: Endnote 5 states that all names were changed to ensure anonymity and endnotes anonymize interviewees by category and number, yet there is no mention of institutional ethics/IRB approval, informed consent procedures, or data protection safeguards despite documenting extra-legal practices (bribery, informal tapping, military/patronage ties) in a sensitive political context.

No qualitative analytical process is described (no information on coding, thematic derivation, triangulation mechanics across archival and interview sources, or handling of discrepant data), although findings are coherently structured and illustrated with direct participant quotes and counter-examples.
domain_ratings.where_found: Research methods and context (PDF Page 8); Results (PDF Pages 10-16)

domain_ratings.justification: Empirical findings on post-formalization shortages and collective/networked repair in Izbet ElHaggana and fragmented developer/state governance, wasta, and decay narratives in New Cairo are clearly presented and explicitly synthesized against the theoretical framework in the Conclusion and Highlights.

domain_ratings.domain_name: How valuable is the research (narrative assessment)
domain_ratings.justification: Substantial theoretical and empirical value: by juxtaposing post-2013 piped formalization in an informal settlement with developer-managed infrastructure in elite New Cairo suburbs, the paper demonstrates why legal connection to state networks does not end informal repair practices (gehood zateya) and illuminates how state and private actors deploy narratives of infrastructural decay.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable contribution to urban water governance and legal-informality scholarship

overall_narrative_summary: Wahby (2021) is a primary qualitative comparative case study investigating water shortages, infrastructural decay narratives, and everyday socio-technical repair practices (gehood zateya) across two settlements on Cairo's eastern desert periphery: the informal settlement of Izbet ElHaggana (following 2013 legal state pipeline installation) and the elite/middle-class district of ElTagammo' ElKhames in New Cairo. Assessed with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study has clear theoretical and empirical aims (Q1), an appropriate qualitative approach (Q2) and comparative two-site design (Q3), clearly articulated findings backed by illustrative vignettes (Q9), and high conceptual value for understanding why formalization and privatization do not displace informal water practices (Q10). However, methodological reporting is thin, yielding five 'Can't tell' ratings across recruitment strategy (Q4), data collection details and cross-site modality differences between in-person ElHaggana fieldwork and virtual/abroad New Cairo interviews (Q5), researcher positionality and use of personal experience in New Cairo (Q6), ethical review and informed consent beyond pseudonymization (Q7), and qualitative coding/analysis procedures (Q8). Overall methodological concern is therefore rated Moderate (5 Can't tell / 0 No items).
overall_rating: Moderate concern (5 Can't tell / 0 No items)
study_design_identified: Qualitative comparative case study (two-phase fieldwork comprising community visits, narrative walks, 72 in-person and virtual interviews, and archival research across two Cairo settlements)
where_found_summary: Research aims and conceptual framing in Abstract (PDF p. 1) and Introduction/Literature Review (PDF pp. 2-6); legal-institutional water sector background in 'The political economy of Cairo's urban waters' (PDF pp. 6-8); study design, two-phase data collection, interview count (n=72), and site selection in 'Research methods and context' (PDF pp. 8-10); empirical findings in 'Results: Repair and decay in Haganna and Tagammo'' (PDF pp. 10-16); synthesis in 'Conclusion' and 'Highlights' (PDF pp. 16-19); anonymization and interviewee citations in 'Notes' 2-27 (PDF pp. 19-20).
why_tool_chosen: The paper reports primary qualitative empirical research based on field visits, narrative walks, archival research, and 72 interviews across two urban case-study sites, with no quantitative dataset or statistical component; the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the protocol-specified appraisal instrument for primary qualitative studies.
